newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA MUST MAKE TOUGH BUDGET CHOICES - OPPOSITION.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA MUST MAKE TOUGH BUDGET CHOICES - OPPOSITION.

text.p: South Africa's Finance Minister Trevor Manuel faces tough choices as he prepares to unveil his 1997/98 budget on March 12, the opposition Democratic Party said on Wednesday.

Finance spokesman Ken Andrew warned that it would be disastrous for the country's long-term future if Manuel did not show convincingly that government was serious about meeting stringent deficit cutting targets.
Andrew said that the government's aim of reducing the deficit to three percent of GDP over the next five years was sound but that could involve some politically unpalatable decisions.
"If the government in any way starts wavering and deviating from its (macro-economic package announced last year)..it's just tickets for this country and this economy," he said.
"Tough and sometimes unpopular judgement calls will have to be made."
To achieve the planned four percent 1997/98 budget deficit, Andrew said that:
- the number of government ministries (and cabinet ministers) should be cut from 25 to 16, saving 200 million rand;
- spending by government departments should be increased by only 4.5 percent a year;
- tax tables should be adjusted to eliminate fiscal drag and the level at which the maximum marginal rate of 45 percent was reached should be raised to 130,000 rand from 100,000 rand;
- value added tax (VAT) should be increased by one percent to 15 percent, netting an extra 2.9 billion rand;
- urgent steps were needed to give the South African Revenue Services full autonomy to improve tax collection;

- government spending should prioritise the fight against crime and 710 million rand should be set aside for the training of the police force and the elimination of backlogs in the courts and prisons;
- new tax relief measures should be introduced to encourage savings;
- an extra 250 million rand should be set aside for university and college student loans and 100 million rand for properly managed AIDS programmes;

- a range of taxes that probably cost more to administer that they yielded should be abolished. These included the secondary tax on companies, donations tax, estate duty and the marketable securities tax;
- six cents, or about 10 percent of the present fuel levy, should be placed in a dedicated road fund to repair rapidly deteriorating roads.

- further savings could come from a 500 million rand cut in the Post Office subsidy, staff cuts in the secret services (400 million rand), the use of fewer consultants (260 million rand), abolition of the South African Communications Service (60 million rand) and "ruthless action" to eliminate illegal payroll payments (at least 250 million rand).
